**The Weight of Silence**

The room is too quiet. Not the kind of quiet that comes with early morning, when the world is still wrapped in the soft gray of dawn, but the kind that settles in like a guest who overstays their welcome. It presses against the walls, thick and suffocating, and I can feel it in my bones—this silence isn’t empty. It’s full. Full of things unsaid, of words that never made it past the throat, of screams that dissolved into the air before they could take shape.

I used to think silence was a void. A blank page. But now I know better. Silence is a living thing. It grows. It feeds. It whispers.

I remember the first time I heard it.

It was a winter night, years ago, when the cold had seeped into the bones of the house. My father was in the kitchen, his back turned to me as he stirred something in a pot. The radio was on, but the volume was low, just enough to fill the space with static and the occasional murmur of a voice. I was sitting at the table, doing homework—or pretending to—when I realized the radio had gone silent. Not the kind of silence where the music cuts out, but the kind where the sound just… vanished. Like someone had reached into the air and plucked the noise away.

I looked up. My father didn’t react. He kept stirring, his shoulders tense, his jaw set. I wanted to ask him what was wrong, but something in the way he held himself told me not to. So I sat there, frozen, listening to the absence of sound as if it were a language I was supposed to understand.

Then, from the corner of the room, a whisper.

It wasn’t a word. Not really. It was more like the sound of a breath held too long, the kind that trembles when it finally lets go. It came from the shadows near the door, where the light from the hallway didn’t quite reach. I turned my head slowly, my pulse hammering in my throat.

Nothing.

Just the empty corner, the flickering bulb of the hallway light casting long, shifting shadows. But the whisper had been real. I *felt* it, like a finger trailing down my spine.

I never told my father about it. Not then. Not ever. Because some things, once spoken, lose their power. And some silences are meant to be kept.

---

Now, sitting in this too-quiet room, I wonder if silence is the only thing that’s ever been honest with me. Words lie. They bend. They twist to fit the shape of what we need to hear. But silence? Silence doesn’t apologize. It doesn’t explain. It just *is*.

And sometimes, it’s all I have left.

I used to fill the silence with noise—music, TV, the hum of a conversation that didn’t matter. But noise is just silence in disguise. A mask. A distraction. It doesn’t drown out the whispers. It just makes them harder to hear.

So I sit. And I listen.

The walls breathe. The floor creaks. The wind outside rattles the windows like it’s trying to get in. And deep in the hollows of the house, something stirs.

I should be afraid. But fear is just another kind of noise.

Maybe that’s why I don’t move. Maybe that’s why I let the silence wrap around me like a second skin. Because in the quiet, for the first time in a long time, I can almost hear myself think.

Almost.
